title: UC Open Source: A System History
text:
Preface
This document tells that story, project by project, from the 1970s to today.
The record comes first. BSD Unix, INGRES, the tz database, the UCSC Genome Browser, Jupyter, Ceph, Apache Spark, RISC-V, Ray, Named Data Networking, PostgreSQL, and others each get their own origin story - the problem, the person, the moment, and what it became. These are not case studies. They are the actual history.
The analysis follows. After you have seen the record, the pattern is hard to miss: UC researchers solved real problems, released the code openly before anyone thought to commercialize it, and watched what happened. What happened was global infrastructure.
The final section addresses what this means now - for the people maintaining this software without support, for the institutions getting credit they have not fully claimed, and for the open source governance moment that AI is forcing on everyone whether they are ready or not.

title: UC Open Source: A System History
section: Who this is for
text:
Who this is for
This document is written for two audiences who do not usually read the same things.
Open source practitioners and OSPO staff will find the full project histories useful - origin dates, key contributors, licensing lineage, and impact numbers that are often scattered across Wikipedia, conference talks, and oral history.
Decision makers - provosts, program officers, foundation staff, research VPs - will find the pattern and stakes sections written for them. The stories are there too, because the stories are the argument.

section: How to use this document

How to use this document
Read it straight through if you want the full arc. Jump to a specific project if you need the origin story for a talk or brief. Share individual chapters - each is written to stand alone.

title: The Internet Itself
section: UCLA and ARPANET: Node 1
text:
UCLA and ARPANET: Node 1
The project: ARPANET (Advanced Research Projects Agency Network) Campus: UCLA Date: October 29, 1969 Key figures: Leonard Kleinrock (faculty), Charley Kline (student programmer), Vint Cerf (grad student), Jon Postel (grad student), Steve Crocker (alumnus)

Section in preparation.


Leonard Kleinrock and Packet Switching
Kleinrock’s contribution was theoretical before it was practical. Traditional telecommunications used circuit switching - a dedicated line from point A to point B, like a phone call. In his MIT doctoral thesis (1962) and his 1964 book, Kleinrock used queueing theory to analyze how messages are delayed in networks that store and forward data (Kleinrock, 1962). Paul Baran at RAND and Donald Davies at Britain’s National Physical Laboratory developed packet-switching designs in separate work (Leiner et al., 1997).
His UCLA lab became the birthplace of the internet’s first node because he had the theory, the equipment, and a team of graduate students who would go on to design the protocols the entire internet runs on.


The Students Who Built the Internet
The graduate students working in Kleinrock’s lab at UCLA in the late 1960s and early 1970s became the architects of the modern internet:
Vint Cerf earned his PhD at UCLA in 1972 and worked in Kleinrock’s group on the Network Measurement Center. At Stanford in 1973-74, he and Bob Kahn of ARPA designed TCP (Cerf & Hochfelder, 1999; Cerf & Kahn, 1974), the protocol that later replaced ARPANET’s original NCP.
Jon Postel went on to manage the DNS (Domain Name System) and the assignment of internet numbers for decades, effectively serving as the internet’s directory administrator. He managed IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) until his death in 1998. His influence over the internet’s naming and numbering systems was so central that it prompted the US government to formalize ICANN as his successor.
Steve Crocker invented the RFC (Request for Comments) process at UCLA in April 1969. RFC 1, written by Crocker, established the open, collaborative process by which internet standards are still developed today. The choice of “Request for Comments” rather than something more authoritative was deliberate - Crocker wanted to encourage participation and avoid having any single voice dominate. Every standard that governs the internet, from email to HTTPS to DNS, exists as an RFC.


Boelter Hall Room 3420
The original IMP, the hardware that made ARPANET’s first node possible, still stands in Boelter Hall Room 3420 at UCLA (UCLA Connection Lab, 2026).

title: The Internet Itself
section: UCSB: Node 3
text:
UCSB: Node 3
Campus: UC Santa Barbara Date: November 1, 1969 Key figures: Glen Culler, Burton Fried
The original four ARPANET nodes were UCLA (Node 1), Stanford Research Institute (Node 2), UC Santa Barbara (Node 3), and the University of Utah (Node 4). Two of the four were UC campuses (Leiner et al., 1997).
Glen Culler and Burton Fried at UCSB were working on interactive mathematics, including methods for displaying mathematical functions (Leiner et al., 1997). Their node went live on November 1, 1969, three days after UCLA’s first message to SRI. UCSB was not a passive recipient of the network; Culler’s team was actively developing applications and pushing on what the network could do.

title: The Internet Itself
section: The Collaboration That Wasn’t Institutional
text:
The Collaboration That Wasn’t Institutional
The people in this chapter knew each other. They communicated through the network they were building. The Network Working Group (RFC process) was genuinely collaborative across institutions - Crocker ran it from UCLA, but contributors came from SRI, UCSB, Utah, and elsewhere. DARPA’s funding created a community that the UC system itself had no formal mechanism to support or recognize.
Lixia Zhang is the living thread. She arrived at the first IETF meeting in 1986 - the successor organization to the ARPANET NWG - as the only woman and the only student in the room. That meeting was populated by the same community that had built the ARPANET. Zhang went on to join UCLA’s faculty and led the Named Data Networking project (Chapter 5). Her career links the founding internet community to internet architecture research at UCLA today.
The UCLA-UCSB-Berkeley collaboration on internet infrastructure happened because DARPA funded it, not because the UC system organized it. The UC OSPO Network is, in part, the belated answer to that gap: a formal mechanism for cross-campus coordination on shared technical infrastructure, fifty years after UC campuses were building the internet without one.

title: The Internet Itself
section: UC Berkeley and TCP/IP: The Implementation That Spread the Protocol
text:
UC Berkeley and TCP/IP: The Implementation That Spread the Protocol
The project: BSD TCP/IP stack (4.2BSD) Campus: UC Berkeley (Computer Systems Research Group, CSRG) Date: 1983 Key figures: Bill Joy (grad student), Sam Leffler, Kirk McKusick, Robert Fabry

Section in preparation.


The Socket API: The Interface That Outlasted Everything
The most durable technical contribution of Berkeley’s TCP/IP implementation was not the protocol stack itself but the socket API, the programming interface that 4.2BSD gave applications for communicating over a network. Joy built the first version of Berkeley’s interprocess communication facilities in 1981, and Joy and Sam Leffler then reworked the interfaces so that several network protocols could run at once (McKusick, 1999). Decades later, Python’s socket module, Node.js networking, Go’s net package, and most network-capable programs expose an interface that traces to this BSD design. You do not think about it; it is just how programs talk to networks.


Why Implementation Mattered as Much as Design
TCP/IP had been designed by Cerf and Kahn (Cerf & Kahn, 1974). What Berkeley did was make it run, make it stable, and make it free with an operating system that universities already had. The DARPA contract to Berkeley was not a minor technical exercise - it was a deliberate strategy to spread the protocol by bundling it with the system universities were already running. It worked. By the time the internet commercialized in the 1990s, the network stack in virtually every Unix system traced to Berkeley’s implementation.
Berkeley’s stack built on an early TCP/IP implementation from Rob Gurwitz at BBN, which Joy integrated and tuned. In the late spring of 1982, Joy left to join Sun Microsystems. Leffler took over and completed the work, and the system was released as 4.2BSD in August 1983 (McKusick, 1999). Sun’s workstations shipped with BSD networking, which carried Berkeley’s TCP/IP implementation into the commercial market.


The Larger Pattern
The UCLA-to-Berkeley TCP/IP story is the earliest instance of the pattern this book documents throughout: UC research producing foundational infrastructure, released openly, that becomes universal. Kleinrock’s theory, Cerf’s protocol design, Berkeley’s implementation - none of it was locked up. All of it spread. The internet is the result.

title: Foundations
section: BSD Unix and the License That Made Open Source Possible
text:
BSD Unix and the License That Made Open Source Possible
The project: Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD Unix) Campus: UC Berkeley Period: 1970s - 1980s Key figures: Bill Joy, Keith Bostic, Marshall Kirk McKusick, and many others

Section in preparation.


What it became
The BSD license - permissive, minimal, requiring only attribution - became the template for how research software gets released. MIT, Apache, and variants of BSD now govern billions of lines of production software. The network stack Berkeley wrote is still in macOS, iOS, and most operating systems.


Why it matters for this history
Every project in this document was made possible by the licensing model Berkeley established. You could release research code, let anyone use it commercially, and watch what happened. BSD Unix proved that worked.

title: Foundations
section: INGRES, POSTGRES, and the Database Lineage
text:
INGRES, POSTGRES, and the Database Lineage
The projects: University INGRES (1973), POSTGRES (1986), PostgreSQL (1995-) Campus: UC Berkeley Key figures: Michael Stonebraker (Turing Award 2014), Eugene Wong, Larry Rowe

Section in preparation.


What it became
INGRES (Stonebraker et al., 1976) spread into industry through its code, its people, and its publications. Its source code was public, and about 1,000 copies went out around the world. Bob Epstein, who worked on INGRES, went on to co-found Britton-Lee and then Sybase (National Research Council, 1999). POSTGRES, Stonebraker’s next Berkeley project, began implementation in 1986. It became Postgres95 and, in 1996, PostgreSQL, which the PostgreSQL Global Development Group still maintains (The PostgreSQL Global Development Group, 2026).


The Stonebraker pattern
Stonebraker’s career at Berkeley established a pattern the rest of this history repeats: solve a real problem in a research lab, release the code openly before it has commercial value, watch the ecosystem form, then commercialize the next generation. He did this with INGRES, which became Ingres Corporation (National Research Council, 1999), and with POSTGRES, which became Illustra, and he continued beyond Berkeley with VoltDB, SciDB, and others.

title: Universal Infrastructure
section: The tz Database: Every Clock on Earth
text:
The tz Database: Every Clock on Earth
The project: tz database (IANA Time Zone Database) Campus: UCLA (Paul Eggert: contributor since 1991, maintainer since 2005, IESG-designated coordinator since 2012) Origin: 1986, Arthur David Olson (NIH) Key figures: Paul Eggert (UCLA), Arthur David Olson

Section in preparation.


What it became
Linux, macOS, iOS, and Android all ship with the tz database. Paul Eggert first worked on it in 1991, when Olson maintained it at NIH (UC Tech News, 2022). He has been its maintainer since 2005 (Eggert, 2026). Every programming language that handles dates and times depends on it. When a country changes its clocks (and they do, constantly - political decisions, wars, referenda), Paul Eggert updates the database and the world’s computers follow.


The lawsuit that almost broke time
In September 2011, Astrolabe Inc. sued Arthur David Olson and Paul Eggert, claiming copyright over historical time zone data (Electronic Frontier Foundation, 2012a). The Electronic Frontier Foundation, with co-counsel at Fish & Richardson, defended them (Electronic Frontier Foundation, 2012b). The database went offline on 7 October 2011. ICANN brought it back online at IANA on 14 October 2011, and Robert Elz served as interim coordinator. Astrolabe dropped the suit on 22 February 2012 (IETF, 2012). The IESG approved Eggert as the Time Zone Coordinator on 13 April 2012 (IESG Secretary, 2012). Olson’s announced retirement had led the IETF to ask ICANN to take over the database (ICANN, 2011). The episode showed how much depended on a very small group of maintainers.

section: Apache HTTP Server: “A Patchy” Web Server
text:
Apache HTTP Server: “A Patchy” Web Server
The project: Apache HTTP Server Campus connection: UC Berkeley (Brian Behlendorf, undergraduate) Period: 1995 - Key figures: Brian Behlendorf (UCB undergrad), Cliff Skolnick, and eight founding contributors

Section in preparation.


What it became
Apache HTTP Server was the most widely used web server for many years. In Netcraft’s December 2015 survey it still ran 50.14% of active sites (Netcraft, 2016). The Apache Software Foundation, which grew from the original group, reported 308 projects in November 2026 (The Apache Software Foundation, 2026), including Apache Spark, which appears later in this history.


The Berkeley connection
Behlendorf’s Berkeley connection is indirect: he was a student there, not running a lab project. But his story illustrates something important about how infrastructure gets built. He was not a professor with a grant. He was an undergrad with a server and a problem. The permissive culture Berkeley embodied - share the code, see what happens - was something he had absorbed.

section: Jupyter: The Procrastination That Runs Science
text:
Jupyter: The Procrastination That Runs Science
The project: IPython / Project Jupyter Campus: UC Berkeley (BIDS) Period: 2001 (IPython, begun at the University of Colorado Boulder (The IPython Development Team, 2026)), 2014 (Project Jupyter) Key figures: Fernando Pérez (creator; UC OSPO Network co-PI), Carol Willing (core developer, ACM Award; not UC-affiliated), Stéfan van der Walt (scikit-image)

Section in preparation.


Carol Willing and the Steering Council
Carol Willing is a core Jupyter developer, three-term Python Steering Council member, and Python Core Developer. She shared the 2017 ACM Software System Award for Jupyter’s global influence - one of computing’s most prestigious recognitions for software that has had lasting impact on the field. Willing was not based at a UC campus. Her role shows how a project that grew at Berkeley drew core contributors from elsewhere.


What it became
Jupyter notebooks (Kluyver et al., 2016) are the dominant interface for interactive scientific computing worldwide. They run in data science courses, AI research labs, public health agencies, and science classrooms. JupyterHub scales the single-user notebook to institutional deployments serving thousands. Binder makes any notebook instantly reproducible and shareable. The format has become a de facto standard for communicating computational science.

On campus today
UC Berkeley, University of Colorado Boulder / UC Berkeley
IPython began in 2001 at the University of Colorado Boulder. Fernando Pérez continued the work at UC Berkeley from 2008. Project Jupyter was announced at SciPy 2014.

Apache Spark: From AMPLab to Apache

Holden Karau and the core team
Holden Karau is a member of the Apache Spark Project Management Committee and a core committer who scaled Spark’s Python and Core engines. She is the co-author of the definitive O’Reilly books Learning Spark and High Performance Spark, which trained a generation of Spark engineers. Karau was not at UC; her Spark work was done in industry, which is part of how a Berkeley project became an industry standard.


What it became
Apache Spark (Zaharia et al., 2012) is the dominant framework for large-scale data processing. It powers data pipelines at virtually every major technology company and research institution. Databricks, founded by members of the Spark team, builds its business on it. The Apache Software Foundation stewards the open-source project; no single company can pull it away.

What it became
RISC-V (Waterman & Asanović, 2019) is an open, royalty-free instruction set architecture. Why this belongs here
NDN is not finished infrastructure - it is active research into what the internet could become. It belongs in this document because NSF funded it as a Future Internet Architecture project led from UCLA, starting with $7.9 million in 2010 (UCLA Henry Samueli School of Engineering, 2010), and because it represents the UC system’s ongoing contribution to internet architecture, not just applications running on top of it.

title: The Pattern
text:
The three-act structure
Nearly every project in this history follows the same arc:

A real problem, solved in a lab. Not a product roadmap. A grad student who needed something to exist. A faculty member frustrated by the limits of current tools.
Release before commercialization. The code went out with a permissive license before anyone had made money from it. This is the Berkeley contribution - not the code alone, but the habit of releasing it.
A neutral home. Apache, Linux Foundation, IANA, the open-source community. Once the code left the lab, it needed somewhere to live that no single company could control. The neutral foundation model is what makes UC research become infrastructure rather than product.
